A.K. Badrul Huq, J: In challenge of rightness of a decision rendered by learned Subordinate Judge, Filth Court, Dhaka in Title suit No. 183 of 1995 making Award dated 07.06.1995 passed by Arbitrators Mr. K. Kamrul Hoda and Mr. Syed Mohsen Ali Rule of Court Appellants Chittagong Steel Mills Limited represented by General Manager/ Project Head and Bangladesh steel Mills Corporation represented by Secretary approached this Court on presentation of this first Miscellaneous Appeal under section No.39(vi) of The Arbitration Act, 1940 (For short The Act) . 

 2. Factual scenario leading to this First Miscellaneous Appeal arising out of Arbitration proceeding may succinctly be taken note of. 

 14. Having felt dissatisfied of the above adjudication Appellants Chittagong Steel Mills Limited approached this Court on setting down this First Miscellaneous Appeal. 

 15. MEC, Dhaka Respondent of First Miscellaneous Appeal as Cross Objector laid Cross objection having la dissatisfied with decision of the learned Subordinate Judge refusing pendente lite interest at the rate of 16% interest on the Award till realization of decretal amount Cross objection has been numbered as Cross Objection No. 5 of 2001. Hearing of the appeal occupied good number of days. Initially Mr. Zubayer Rahman Chowdhury argued the appeal for Appellants but since he was elevated to Bench Mr. Md. Khalilur Rahman and Ms. Rubaiyat Hossain learned Counsels argued the appeal. First Respondent is represented by Mr. Omar Sadat along with Mr. Abdul Halim, learned Counsels. 

 18. Headmost ground and contention surged forward is that the Arbitrators misconducted Arbitration proceeding and Court committed a patent illegality in not setting aside the Award on declining to make it Rule of Court. 

 19. Ground urged and contention pressed have been spurned from the side of Respondent raising contention that Arbitrators did not at all misconduct in conducting Arbitration proceeding and learned Subordinate Judge, also, did not find any misconduct on the part of Arbitrators by which the Award could he set aside. 

 20. What amounts to "Misconduct"? It is difficult to define exhaustively and exactly what amounts to "Misconduct" on the part of an Arbitrator. The expression is of wide import. 

 21. Webster has defined "Misconduct" as: to conduct a miss; to mismanage: wrong or improper conduct had behavior: unlawful behaviour or conduct. It has defined the term misconducted himself as to behave improperly. 

 22. In Corpus Juris Secundum Vo. 58 page 818 "Misconduct" is stated hereunder: 

 "Both in law and in ordinary speech the term "misconduct" usually implies an act done with a wrong intention and conveys the idea of intentional wrongdoing. The term implies fault beyond the error of judgment: a wrongful intention and not a mere error of judgment; but it does not necessarily imply corruption or criminal intention and in the legal idea of misconduct, an evil intention is not a necessary ingredient." 

 23. In halsbury's Laws of England. Third Edition. Volume-II page 57 it is stated: "the  expression 'misconduct' is "of wide import" and includes: 

 "on the one hand bribery and corruption and on the other hand a mere mistake as to the scope of authority conferred by the agreement of reference or an error of law appearing on the lace of the award . Thus misconduct occurs if the arbitrator or umpire as the case may he, fails to decide all the matters which are referred to him; if by his award he purports to decide matters which have not, in fact been included in the agreement of reference; if the award is inconsistent." 

 24. The words "misconducted the proceedings". in the words of Lord Atkin J., mean "such a mishandling of the arbitration as is likely to cause some substantial miscarriage of justice and one instance of this is where arbitrator refuses to hear evidence upon a material issue Williams Vs Wills 83 L.J. K.13. 1299 (1229). 

 25. The word "Misconduct" means mishandling of Arbitration proceeding causing displacement of Rules of Justice and lack of integrity and impartiality any neglect of duty on the part of the Arbitrator which is likely to lead a substantial miscarriage of Justice. 

 26. One of the "Misconduct" highlighted from the side of Appellants was that claim of Respondent was for Taka. 14.50 lacy as made out in the petition and also, the Legal Notice and the Award in respect of Taka. 58.00.000.00 by Arbitrators was illegal and this illegality constitute a "Misconduct". 

 29. Arbitrators took into stock this clause 11 of the agreement and found that Respondent was entitled for an amount of Taka 14.50 thousand + 43.50 lacs - 58,00.000.00. It cannot be,  thus , said that there was no basis for awarding an amount of Taka 58.00,000.00 as Award money and this Award money of Taka 58.00.000.00 cannot be at all characterized to be a misconduct on the part of Arbitrators. Award amount is very much in consonance of the Clause 11 of the agreement. 

 30. The other "Misconduct" canvassed was that Respondent was not an exclusive sales agent and Respondent as not entitled to claim of any commission whatsoever from Appellants. 

 exclusive sale commission agent by the Appellants for supplying C.S.M. products to Bangladesh Defence Services. Contention advanced that Respondent was not exclusive sales commission agent holds no water and it stands rejected. Plea of "Misconduct" on the part of Respondent MEC, Dhaka, thus, stands flung to the wind. 

 35. Another limb of "Misconduct" attributed is that Award was passed on misconception 

 Arbitrator is not hound by technicalities of The Evidence Act and he does not adjudicate nor does he sit as a Court or Tribunal. Proceeding before Arbitrator need not he conducted with such meticulous care as is required in ordinary Court of law. So long as there is substantial compliance with the principles of natural justice. Arbitration Award cannot he quashed simply on the ground of misreading of evidence. Arbitrators in Awarding Award had taken upon themselves the duties of Arbitrators carefully and considered papers in the case and passed the Award. It, thus, cannot be at all suggested that the Award rested on no evidence or on 

 37. Learned Subordinate Judge, also, carefully examined the Award, petition presented by Respondent and objection tiled by Appellants, materials on record and fact and circumstances of the case and found that Arbitrators did not misconduct themselves in conducting Arbitration proceeding and in pronouncement of Award. 

 42. This takes us to a vehement argument put forward from the side of Respondent that under section 33 of The Act deposit of Award money or furnishment of security by a Bank Guarantee is a must and unless this requirement is complied with strictly there will be no objection in the eye of law and Court is bound to make the Award Rule of Court and whether Arbitrator misconducted or not could not be looked into in absence of deposit under section 33 of The Act and Appellants as a requirement of law furnished Bank Guarantee as security for the Award money for a limited, period and Bank guarantee was extended from 24.10.1995 to 23.10.2001 and, thereafter , Bank guarantee was not extended nor further validated and since Bank Guarantee had neither been extended nor been validated furnishment of security for Award money stands as no security and no compliance of section 33 of The Act. In support of the contention a certified copy of the Bank Guarantee submitted before learned Subordinate Judge had been placed before us Bangladesh Water Development Board Vs. Nasim and Brothers and another, 1988 BLD HCD 369, Bangladesh Water Development Board and others Vs. Pragati Prakaushali and another, 49 DIA 11CD 335, Mol Enterprise Inc. Vs. Government of The People's Republic of Bangladesh , 4 BLC HCD 407 and Rajdhani Unnayan Katripakkha (Rajuk) Vs. M.N. Alam and Associates Ltd. and another , 54 DLR HCD 161 have been relied upon in support of contention. 

 (a) that an arbitrator or umpire has misconducted himself or the proceedings 

 54. Ground (h) is not relevant I'm our purpose. Ground (a) i.e. Misconduct had been dealt with earlier and it has been positively held that there had not been any misconduct on the part of the Arbitrators in delivering Award. 

 55. Expression expressed in clause (c) is an Award which has been improperly procured or is otherwise invalid. In In re whitely and Roberts Arbitration (1891) 1 Ch 558 it has been held that an award is improperly made when it is made by collusion or in consequence of a bribe. In Amarnath Vs. Echhal. AIR 1932 Lahore 378 = 137 I.C. 846 it has been laid down that the words "an arbitration has been improperly procured" include the case of an arbitrator who has been illegally and improperly appointed. No allegation had been mounted against the Arbitrators that Award had been obtained by collusion or inconsequence of a bribe. No plea had been taken that the Arbitrators had been biased and partial . Personal misconduct of the Arbitrators had not been also demonstrated. It cannot he also said that Arbitrators had been illegally and improperly appointed. The two Arbitrators had been appointed in terms of Clause 17 of the agreement. 

 58. Learned Subordinate Judge also on a proper consideration of all materials and facts and circumstances of the case accepted the Award as a valid one and accordingly made the Award Rule of Court. No exception can be taken to the decision rendered by learned Subordinate Judge in making Award Rule of Court. 

 65. In WA PDA and another Vs. Messrs Khanzada Muhammad Abdul Haque Khan Khattak and Company(Supra) applicability of the provisions of Order XLI, Rule 33 of The Code of Civil Procedure to award interest on award which was required to be passed by the trial court was mooted and decided. In the case a good number of authorities of Pakistan and Indian jurisdiction had been attended to. Taking into stock the principles enunciated in good number of authorities of Pakistan and Indian jurisdiction and also, taking into stock the provisions of section 29 of The Arbitration Act and also, the provisions of Order XLI, Rule 33 of The Code of Civil Procedure it had been held: 

 If the trial court had not awarded interest as provided in section 29 of The Arbitration Act, the appellate court has/had ample powers under Order XLI, Rule 33 of The Code of Civil Procedure to pass any decree and make any order which ought to have been passed or made and to pass or make such further or other decree or order as the case may require and this power could be exercised by the court in favour of all or any of the respondents or parties although such respondents or parties may not have filed any appeal or objection. 

 66. In Secretary, Irrigation Department, Government of Orissa and others Vs. G.C. Roy (Supra)-The Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court of India summed up the legal position in regard to grant of interest pendente lite in the following terms: "The question still remains whether arbitrator has the power to award interest pendente lite , and if so, on what principle . We must reiterate that we are dealing with the situation where the agreement does not provide for grant of such interest nor does it prohibit such grant in other words we are dealing with a case where the agreement is silent as to award of interest. On a conspectus of aforementioned decisions the following principles emerge: 

 (i) A person deprived of the use of money to which he is legitimately entitled has a right to be compensated for the deprivation call it by any name. It may be called interest, compensation or damages. This basic consideration is as valid for the period the dispute is pending before the arbitrator as it is for the period prior to the arbitrator entering upon the reference. This is the principle of Section 34, Civil Procedure Code and there is no reason or principle to hold otherwise in the case of arbitrator. 

 (iv) Over the years the English and Indian courts have acted on the assumption that where the agreement does not prohibit and a party to the reference makes a claim for interest. The arbitrator must have the power to award interest pendente lite. Thawardas has not been followed in the later decisions of this. Court. It has been explained and distinguished on the basis that in that case there was no claim for interest but only a claim for unliquidated damages. It has been said repeatedly that observations in the said judgment were not intended to lay down any such absolute or universal rule as they appear to, on first impression. Until Jena case almost all the courts in the country had upheld the power of the arbitrator to award interest pendente lite Continuity and certainty is a highly desirable feature of law. 

 "Where the agreement between the parties does not prohibit grant of interest and where a party claims interest and that dispute (along with the claim for principal amount or independently) is referred to the arbitrator he shall have the power to award interest pendente lite. This is for the reason that in such a case it must be presumed that interest was an implied term of the agreement between the parties and therefore when the parties refer all their disputes or refer the dispute as to interest as such- to the arbitrator he shall have the power to award interest. This does not mean that in every case the arbitrator should necessarily award interest pendente lite. It is a matter within his discretion to be exercised in the light of all the facts and circumstances of the case keeping the ends of justice in view." 

 authorities both of our jurisdiction and foreign jurisdiction such as Eddowes Vs. Hopkins , (1780) 99 All England reports, Bengal Nagpur Rly Co. Vs. Ratanji Ramji AIR (1938) (PC) 70, AZ. Co. Vs. SM Bakhsh 17 DLR (SC) 404, Secretary, Irrigation Department Vs. GC Roy (Supra), Md. Emus VS. University of Chittagong, 44 DLR (AD) 296 and other authorities. In the case provision and scope of section 29 of The Arbitration Act section 34 of The Code of Civil Procedure, section 61 of the sale of Goods Act and section 73 of The Contract Act had been taken into account. 

 An Arbitrator may allow pendente lite interest on the analogy of the Court's power to grant interest if the dispute were agitated before it. In the case of Arbitrator, this interest should be for a period not exceeding four months. This period of four months as referred to in section 3 of the First Schedule of the Arbitration Act, is fixed for concluding an Arbitration proceeding; this period for concluding the proceeding may, of course, he extended by Court; but such extension will not necessarily empower the Arbitrator to allow interest for a period beyond four months unless the Arbitrator finds that the debtor or the person from whom money is due has deliberately prolonged the arbitration proceeding. In other words, the Arbitrator may allow interest pendente Ike for a period beyond four months if the prolongation of the proceeding is caused by circumstances beyond his control. Again to avoid any controversy the period for pendente lite interest will start from the date on which the Arbitrator enters upon the arbitration proceedings and end on the day the award is made.
